On my recent piece:

I read this generous critique with interest, but I suspect that the central argument of my analysis has not been fully understood. Huntington’s Clash of Civilizations rests on a fundamental premise: that Western civilization remains sufficiently coherent, self-assured, and conscious of its own identity to recognize itself as engaged in a civilizational confrontation with another.

My contention, informed in part by personal experience, is that Western civilization, or perhaps more precisely its European and U.S. expressions, is itself undergoing a profound crisis of identity and confidence. Civilizations in such a condition often lose the capacity to distinguish their own struggles from those of others. They become susceptible to internalizing external antagonisms, gradually transforming foreign conflicts into domestic ones.

Islam, meanwhile, is engaged in an intense struggle within itself, between competing theological, political, and civilizational visions. I believe these internal antagonisms will deepen over the coming decades. The more consequential question, however, is what happens when a Western civilization already beset by its own existential uncertainties becomes entangled in these struggles, absorbing them into its political and intellectual life.

This is where my analysis departs most fundamentally from Huntington. The defining civilizational confrontation of our time may not be one between a confident West and an external Islamic civilization, but one in which a fractured West increasingly becomes the arena in which the internal conflicts of another civilization are fought.

Book recommendation:

Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Turgenev, Chekhov, and many others read Goncharov’s Oblomov and Lenin repeatedly invoked Oblomov in his writings and speeches as  the ultimate symbol of Russian inertia. Unfortunately, I don’t think this novel receives nearly the recognition it deserves. In my eyes, it’s the greatest Russian novel ever written.

There’s something eternal about it. The tension between grand aspirations and complete passivity, the seductions of opulence, the inability to act even when one knows perfectly well what must be done. There are echoes of it in French literature, particularly in Flaubert’s Bouvard et Pécuchet and Huysmans’s À rebours, where retreat from the world and the pursuit of an ideal existence become their own forms of imprisonment.

Although Goncharov was writing about distinctly Russian problems, I’ve always found something profoundly late-imperial/something recurrent about Oblomov. A society so accustomed to comfort, so absorbed in its habits and fantasies, that it gradually loses the will to act. 

More importantly, what makes the novel so captivating is how easily one can understand Oblomov’s desires. Who hasn’t imagined a life in which comfort, leisure, and freedom from obligation are the ultimate goals? But what happens when the very comfort you spend your life pursuing ends up eating you alive?

Explorers

$SYH – Drilling has begun at Getty East in a Denison-funded program at Russell Lake. I like the combination of flagship exploration and partner-funded work, with assays from this campaign the next thing to watch.

Producers

$HL – Lucky Friday’s record output in the last reported quarter remains a reason I hold Hecla among my preferred silver producers. The next operating report needs to show that strength continuing across the business.

$PAAS – An updated reserve estimate put silver reserves at roughly 511M oz. Cash generation and La Colorada Skarn remain the attractions; Q3 results are due in November.

Explorers & Developers

$GRSL.V – San Marcial drilling continues to support the case for resource growth. I’m looking for more step-outs and an updated picture of the deposit’s scale.

$JTWO – My wildcard. Sierra Plata’s surface work identified seven veins and strong silver samples. Trenching, permits and eventual drilling are the next tests; surface samples are still early evidence.

🟠 COPPER

$CGNT.V – My primary copper exposure. Mocoa drilling returned another long copper-equivalent intersection, and the company has outlined targets beyond the current resource. Continued drilling and the planned preliminary economic assessment are what I’m watching.

⚫ GRAPHENE

$HG $HGRAF – Still my largest holding. HydroGraph showcased its Fractal Graphene Paste in October and has proposed a U.S. redomicile vote later this month. Texas scale-up and converting customer work into commercial orders remain the catalysts that matter most to me.

📅 October 11, 2026 | Looking ahead to October 12–16
Four metals. One busy week ahead. Inflation, the dollar and Chinese demand could set the tone.

☢️ URANIUM
The uranium price reference tracked by Trading Economics ended Friday around $90/lb. Fuel supply constraints and expanding nuclear ambitions remain supportive, but mining equities still need buying momentum.

Silver climbed 2.4% to around $60.77 in Friday’s late trading. A strong rebound—but next week’s inflation test matters.

🔶 COPPER
China’s smelters face shortages of both concentrate and scrap. Reuters reports that planned October–November maintenance could remove roughly 80,000 tonnes of refined supply. That keeps the supply side firmly in focus.

Next week: Watch Chinese buying, exchange inventories and supply disruption headlines. My expectation is a tug-of-war between constrained supply and concerns about demand at elevated prices.

🥇 GOLD
Gold recovered to around $4,194 in Friday’s late trading, heading for a weekly gain of roughly 1.3%. Bargain buying helped after the midweek selloff.

Next week: Can the rebound survive the inflation data? Cooler numbers could support gold through lower yields; hotter numbers could revive pressure from expectations of further rate hikes.

🗓️ THE WEEK’S BIG TESTS
• Wednesday, October 14: US CPI
• Thursday, October 15: PPI, retail sales and regional manufacturing surveys
• Friday, October 16: Industrial production

My outlook: Expect volatility around the data. I’m watching whether precious metals sustain their rebound, copper’s supply constraints translate into strength, and uranium equities attract fresh buying.

I do believe this would be very popular concept for retail to invest in, given how simple it is to understand

𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗜𝘀 𝗢𝗻𝗲 - 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗼𝗳 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆

𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭. 𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦.

-Tibetan Buddhist teacher

Over the last couple of weeks, I have been exploring a thought experiment that has taken me deeper and deeper into the Self.

The more I observe life, the more waking reality reminds me of a dream.

Of course, dreams and waking life follow different laws. But that is not the point.

Nobody has ever returned from the grave to tell us what happens after death. Yes, there are stories of people who were declared clinically dead and later revived. But perhaps the doctors were mistaken about their condition, or perhaps their hearts had stopped while their brains had not yet suffered irreversible damage. None of this proves that someone has experienced irreversible death and returned.

So, having never experienced death myself, I am left with the closest experience I have: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲.

When we dream, everything feels real. People, animals, trees, love, fear, anger, desire. An entire world exists, and we believe in it completely.

Then we wake up.

Suddenly, we realize that the people, the trees, the animals, and even the person we believed ourselves to be were all made of the same fabric.

𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲.

And perhaps this is the simplest way to understand the ancient idea that 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗢𝗻𝗲.

The most fascinating part is that I was no more real than anyone else in my dream. I wasn’t the one real person surrounded by imaginary characters. 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗼𝗼.

Today, walking through the streets of Istanbul, I watched hundreds of people passing by. Different faces, different lives, different desires. Everyone seemingly living inside their own reality.

And I asked myself: 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝗜 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺?

I assume these people have their own inner experience, just as I do. But I cannot directly know their awareness, any more than I can know the awareness of characters inside my dreams.

It’s a fair point regarding bragging, but I believe bragging serves a purpose.

In our business, people like Michael Burry and countless others on X write intelligently and eloquently, attracting tens or even hundreds of thousands of followers. Yet you often have no idea what their actual track records look like or how good they really are.

I suspect that if many of these people published their returns over the past ten years, they would have significantly underperformed the market, and far fewer people would follow them.

People publish convincing ideas, and readers simply assume they know what they’re doing. But writing intelligently and making money in the market are two very different skills.

Since people often find it difficult to believe that valuable information can be free, I occasionally share my returns to demonstrate that my ideas actually generate alpha. They’re not just clever theories I throw into the ether.

Those posts also attract more people to my account, which helps my ideas reach a wider audience.

I don’t want anyone to follow me blindly. Quite the opposite. I want people to see the results, become curious, investigate my ideas, and do their own research.

Ultimately, I’m trying to bring a little more transparency and integrity to a space where eloquent writing is too often mistaken for investment skill.

Ideas are easy to publish. Generating alpha consistently is a different story.
